explanation: Rule of thumb: checkout the receiver, then call the sender: `git switch main && git merge feature`.
tip: If you merge from the wrong branch, use `git merge --abort` immediately.

explanation: Fast-forward creates a straight linear history without unnecessary merge bubbles.
tip: It's the cleanest merge type for short-lived personal feature branches.

explanation: 3-way merge uses: base ancestor + branch A tip + branch B tip.
tip: The resulting commit has two parents instead of one.

explanation: `--no-ff` makes it obvious in history that a feature was developed as an isolated branch.
tip: Many large teams enforce `--no-ff` for pull requests.

explanation: `-d` is your safety belt: Git prevents you from deleting unmerged code.
tip: If Git says 'The branch is not fully merged', check your commits before using `-D`.

explanation: `-D` force deletes. Use it only when you intentionally want to discard an abandoned experiment.
Branches represent active tasks. When the task is done, the branch should be retired.
tip: GitHub even offers an automatic 'Delete branch' button on merged PRs.

explanation: You can also use GitHub's web interface to delete remote branches with one click.
Commits are reachable from `main`, so they remain permanently in your repo history.
tip: This is why Git branches are so fearless to delete.

explanation: `git log --graph --oneline --all` is many developers' favorite alias.
